tagline.text: The stone church in Malolos where Asia's first republican constitution was born

items.credit: Ramon FVelasquez / CC BY-SA 3.0 / Wikimedia Commons

children.text: A church in Malolos, Bulacan, where the Malolos Congress convened in 1898 and drafted Asia's first republican constitution — a Philippine national shrine known as the "Cradle of Democracy in the Orient." Just 1–2 hours from Manila, it's well suited to a half-day history trip combining the basilica and a street of old mansions.
Barasoain Church is a Catholic church in Malolos City, the capital of Bulacan province, about
45km

north of Manila. Its formal name is Our Lady of Mount Carmel Parish, and "Barasoain" comes from the name of a village in Navarre, Spain, the hometown of the Archbishop of Manila at the time. It's an image every Filipino has seen at some point, in textbooks and on banknotes alike.
What makes this church special is that it was the stage for the Philippine Revolution. The revolutionary forces fighting Spain convened the first Philippine Congress, the Malolos Congress, here on
September 15, 1898
, and the resulting Malolos Constitution was promulgated on
January 21, 1899
. Two days later, on
January 23, 1899

, the First Republic (the Malolos Republic), with Emilio Aguinaldo as president, was inaugurated at this church. As Asia's first case of a colony under Western rule drafting its own republican constitution, it earned the nickname "the Cradle of Democracy in the Orient."
The current building was rebuilt in brick and stone from
to

after earlier churches on the site were destroyed by fire and earthquakes, and it's marked by a weighty facade blending Baroque and Renaissance Revival styles and a multi-tiered bell tower. The church was declared a national shrine in

, and the old convent building now houses a museum run by the National Historical Commission of the Philippines (NHCP). For the revolution's centennial in 1998, President Joseph Estrada was even inaugurated here.

The church alone takes about an hour to see, but within walking distance are Malolos Cathedral, once used as the presidential palace; Casa Real, now a museum of Philippine political history; and the Kamestisuhan district, lined with Spanish-era mansions — making a good half-day history walk. Recommended for travelers interested in Philippine modern history, families wanting to show children Philippine history, and expats looking for a day trip near Manila.

blocks.title: Taking in the facade and bell tower

children.text: The moss-covered gray stone facade, round rose window, and bell tower with exposed red brick together form the scene straight out of Philippine textbooks. From across the plaza, you can frame the facade and bell tower in a single shot.

blocks.title: The nave where the Malolos Congress convened

children.text: This very nave is where delegates of the revolutionary congress, led by president Pedro Paterno, gathered to debate the constitution. Walk through the interior, decorated with white columns, gilded ornamentation, and chandeliers, and picture that day. Please refrain from viewing during Mass.

The old convent beside the church houses a museum run by the National Historical Commission, displaying the history of the Malolos Congress and the First Republic along with materials on the revolution's leaders. You can also see the parish museum's exhibits on the church's history and sacred relics.
About
10–15 minutes
on foot south of Barasoain, this cathedral served as President Aguinaldo's residence and office during the First Republic. Take in the old trees in the churchyard along with the facade.

A Spanish-era government building, now a museum of Philippine political history run by the National Historical Commission. See exhibits on the Malolos Republic-era printing press, Aguinaldo's personal effects, and the "20 Women of Malolos" to whom Rizal wrote a letter.

The area around the cathedral clusters 19th-century mansions once home to wealthy Spanish-Chinese mestizo families, giving the district its name, "Kamestisuhan" (mestizo town). Stroll slowly through the lanes, where wooden windows and stone foundations still remain.
Barasoain Church appeared on the old 1-peso and 10-peso notes, and on the front of the 200-peso note, the
edition shows the church facade, while from the
edition it shows the nave interior within a scene of the opening of the Malolos Congress. Printing of the 200-peso note ended in
, so it's rare to see, but if you get hold of one, comparing it against the real nave is a small pleasure.

Biak-na-Bato is where the revolutionary forces founded the Republic of Biak-na-Bato in 1897, so pairing it with Malolos lets you trace the course of the Philippine Revolution in a single day. A private or chartered vehicle makes for an easier, unhurried trip.
Buses bound for Malolos, Baliwag, and Hagonoy run frequently from Cubao and Caloocan's Monumento in Manila. Depending on traffic, it takes about
1 hour 30 minutes–2 hours
, for a fare of about
. Get off at Malolos Crossing and continue about
10–15 minutes
more to the church by jeepney or tricycle.
Jeepneys to Malolos from Monumento are slow but cheap (about
). Just ask the driver to let you off at "Barasoain."
Take NLEX and exit toward Guiguinto, then continue into downtown Malolos — about
1 hour–1 hour 30 minutes
from northern Manila. There's paid parking along the streets and near the plaza around the church.
Grab runs about
one way from downtown Manila, and since it can be hard to catch a ride back in town, a round-trip charter is sometimes more convenient.

The North–South Commuter Railway (NSCR), linking Manila's Tutuban to Malolos, is under construction. Once it opens, Malolos Station will be close to the church, so check the latest notices on service status before you visit.
Under the schedule the government adjusted in
September 2026
, partial operation of the Valenzuela–Malolos section is targeted for
December 2027
and full Clark–Calamba service for
. Until then you'll need to go by bus or private car.
From Barasoain Church to Malolos Cathedral and Casa Real is under
1km
, so you can walk it. On a hot day, take a tricycle instead (about
for a short trip).
Since much of the visit is indoors at the church and museums, you can go any time of year, but for walking the old streets, the dry season,
November–April
, is best.
December–February
is relatively cool, good even for a midday walk, and
March–May
sees temperatures climb to
, so it's best to get moving early in the morning.
During the wet season,
June–October
, afternoon showers are frequent, and when a typhoon passes through, Bulacan's low-lying areas and roads can flood. As for historical events, commemorations are held around
September 15
, marking the Malolos Congress's opening, and around
January 23
, marking the First Republic's inauguration, while the Malolos Santo Niño Festival procession fills the streets on the
last Sunday of January
. A church feast is also held around
July 16
, the feast day of Our Lady of Mount Carmel, the parish's patron saint.

Most travelers visit Malolos as a day trip from Manila, so there's rarely a need to stay overnight. If you're combining the trip with Biak-na-Bato or Pampanga to the north, one option is to stay at a business hotel in downtown Malolos or near a shopping mall (about
per night) and continue north the next day.

Bulacan is one of the Philippines' foremost pastry and dessert regions. Malolos ensaymada, piled high with butter and cheese; inipit, a sweet filling between thin pastry layers; the crisp cracker otap; and pastillas de leche, made from reduced milk, are the signature snacks and make great gifts. For meals, local restaurants around the church and cathedral serve tangy sinigang, braised pork adobo, and Bulacan-style rice noodle dishes. Downtown malls also have plenty of chain restaurants and cafes.
The National Historical Commission museums are often closed on Mondays. Check operating days and hours (usually around
8 AM–4 PM
) before you visit.
Weekends bring many weddings and baptisms, which can limit access to the nave. Weekday mornings are quieter.
Inside the church, avoid sleeveless tops and short shorts, and refrain from taking photos during Mass.
When leaving from Manila, get on NLEX before
7 AM
or after
9 AM
to avoid rush-hour traffic.
For facade photos, shoot in the morning when the sun lights the front of the church, to avoid backlighting.

Pairing this with the Aguinaldo Shrine in Cavite (the site of the independence declaration) makes it easier to follow the story from the 1898 declaration of independence to the 1899 founding of the Republic.
Snacks like ensaymada and pastillas often sell out by afternoon at many shops, so buy them in the morning.
The National Historical Commission museum next to the church (the 1899 Republic Museum) has no admission fee and usually shows a light-and-sound show of about
7 minutes
, recreating the Malolos Congress with life-size figures, at
10 AM
and
3 PM
. Going at show time makes the exhibits much easier to understand.
Barasoain Church is still an active church holding Mass, as well as a national shrine. Pause your visit during Mass and ceremonies, and don't touch the altar or relics.
Museum hours and exhibits can change for renovations or events, so check the latest notices.
Around Malolos Crossing and the market, crowds make pickpocketing a risk.
In the wet season, some days bring flooding on downtown streets, so check typhoon forecasts and adjust your plans.
Agree on the tricycle fare before you get in.
In the rainy season, when rain and high tide coincide, central Malolos often floods for days at a time. On
too, southwest monsoon rain filled even the floor of Barasoain Church, so if you go in
July–September
, check the previous day's news on flooding in Bulacan.
